So for Putin, it made sense to wait. You know, let's just wait. I may get what I want without having to do very much to get it. Well, thankfully, Trump did not win. Even more thankfully, Biden and his team were able to begin to knit together the transatlantic alliance and particularly NATO. And I think that was a surprise to Putin because when he invaded He thought, number one, he could once again sort of fool the rest of the world through what's called a false flag operation and was actually planning to try to set up some encounter so that it looked like Ukrainians had attacked his people, his troops or his people, which would have then given him an excuse. And brilliantly, our intelligence community working with the intelligence communities of our allies, you know, reveal that information and that prevented Putin from being able to disguise his invasion. So the other thing that happened is that when you're a dictator, when you're a leader for life, as he now is, people only tell you what they think you want to hear. So all of his intelligence about Ukraine was it would be cakewalk, no problem, you'd be in key even a week, you would, you know, behead the government, basically take it over, install a puppet, all would be well. And he didn't count on the bravery and the courage and the frankly smarts of the Ukrainian government and people to defend themselves. So where we are now is, I don't think there's any end to this that is really in our interests other than what can be fairly perceived as a Ukrainian victory. Now, what does that mean? Well, if Ukraine can take back the territory that it has lost in the invasion starting in 2022, which would then exclude Crimea and the Donbass, there might be an opportunity to persuade the Ukrainians to enter into some kind of negotiations or to view it as a frozen conflict in return for NATO troops being stationed on their borders. At this point, I don't think Ukraine would accept that. I think Ukraine is now determined under Zelensky's leadership to try to get as much of their territory back as possible. But it's a slog, Hank. It's a slog. And everybody's running out of literally ammunition And we have done a lot to support Ukraine, but it's only been shy of 5% of our defense budget. And it has been a necessary action to protect ourselves and to protect our already existing NATO allies. So right now, I think we have to do everything we can to help Ukraine take as much territory back as possible. And then in the winter, kind of near the two-year mark, take stock of where we are.

turn_text: Oh, I think about this a lot. You know, I now have three grandchildren. I think you have four, Hank. And I think mine are a lot younger than yours. So clearly, I am pretty obsessed with what's going to happen to young people in our country and elsewhere around the world. And I have a lot of young people who work for me and a lot of young people I interact with at the Clinton Foundation and the Clinton Global Initiative and other of my activities. And I get asked all the time, what I think is going to happen or how they can best maneuver in a quite uncertain world from their perspective. And I guess I would say a couple of things. I mean, I always start with education. There is no way to prevent change happening in the world. We are seeing it at an increasingly rapid pace. We have no idea what artificial intelligence is going to do to us for us going forward. And just to be as well educated, to be as well prepared as you possibly can, because that's the only insurance policy that you have to try to navigate a fast-changing world like the one we are in. Secondly, get off your screens, get out into the real world, spend time with real people, your friends, neighbors, volunteer at your church or synagogue or community organization, and be a really careful consumer of social media. Do not go down those rabbit holes that the algorithms are addicting you to and sending you down. No good can come of that. And it can also undermine your own self-confidence and your own sense of identity. Find a way to serve. And, you know, there's all kinds of ways to serve you and I have been fortunate to be in public service. Some people are in military service. Some people are in, you know, a form of, you know, faith-based service or community activities. find a way to serve. And even if it's just working at a food bank, you know, a couple hours on a Saturday afternoon, find a way to get out of your comfort zone, get out of your bubble and go out and be with other people. And I guess finally, you know, follow your dream and your passion. And nobody can tell you what that is. That has to come from who you are, what's inside of you. But keep searching until you find it. And of course, you want to make a good living. Of course, you want to have enough, you know, financial resources to, you know, make decisions for yourself and maybe in the future of family. but also make sure what you're doing in your professional world, your career, your workplace is satisfying because life goes by really fast. And if you look back, it's like that wonderful book written by Rabbi Harold Kushner, which starts with the line, nobody on his deathbed ever says, I wish I'd spent more time at the office. I mean, fine. other sources of meaning and purpose in your life and you know that doesn't mean it's the same thing for your entire life hopefully a long life but you know get started and and find your way forward and find it with purpose and joy.
